questions.q: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), replacing the Indian Penal Code 1860, came into force on:
o: 26 January 2024
1 July 2024
15 August 2024
25 December 2023
questions.src: The BNS came into force on 1 July 2024, though it received Presidential assent on 25 December 2023.

questions.q: "Actus Reus" and "Mens Rea," the two general elements of a crime, refer respectively to:
o: The punishment and the sentence
The guilty ACT and the guilty MIND/mental element
The victim and the accused
The prosecution and the defence
questions.src: Actus Reus is the physical/external act element; Mens Rea is the mental/fault element — both generally required together for criminal liability.

questions.q: Among the four Stages of Crime (Intention, Preparation, Attempt, Commission), which stage is generally NOT punishable, except in specified offences?
o: Attempt
Commission
Intention and (generally) Preparation
None of these stages are ever punishable
questions.src: Mere intention is never punishable alone; preparation is generally not punishable except for specific offences (e.g., preparing to wage war) — Attempt and Commission are generally punishable.

questions.q: Under Section 20 BNS, a child UNDER 7 years of age:
o: Can be held fully criminally liable like an adult
Has ABSOLUTE incapacity — nothing done by them is an offence
Is liable only for serious offences
Requires a court hearing to determine liability case by case
questions.src: Section 20 creates an absolute, irrebuttable incapacity for children under 7 — nothing they do is an offence.

questions.q: Under Section 21 BNS, a child ABOVE 7 and UNDER 12 years is excused from criminal liability if they:
o: Are always fully liable regardless of maturity
Have not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of the act
Are excused only if a parent testifies on their behalf
This age group has no special provision at all
questions.src: Section 21 creates a qualified, rebuttable incapacity based on a maturity-of-understanding test for this age group.

questions.q: Under Section 34 BNS, the foundational principle of private defence states:
o: Private defence is never a valid excuse for any act
Nothing is an offence which is done in exercise of the right of private defence
Private defence only applies to property, never to the body
Private defence requires prior police permission
questions.src: Section 34 is the foundational statement that a properly-exercised private defence act carries no criminal liability.

questions.q: In Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab (2010), the Supreme Court held that the right of private defence:
o: Requires an offence to have ACTUALLY been committed before it can be exercised
Arises from a mere REASONABLE APPREHENSION of danger — an actual offence need not have occurred
Can never justify causing death under any circumstances
Is only available to police officers
questions.src: Darshan Singh established that reasonable apprehension alone triggers the right, without requiring the offence to actually occur first.

questions.q: Following Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab, a person exercising private defence under sudden attack is:
o: Expected to calculate a mathematically precise, proportionate response
NOT expected to modulate their defence with mathematical precision, given the excitement and confusion of the moment
Required to first attempt to flee before defending themselves in every case
Automatically guilty regardless of the circumstances
questions.src: The Court explicitly rejected demanding "mathematical precision" from someone acting under the genuine stress of sudden danger.

questions.q: Under Section 37 BNS, the right of private defence does NOT extend to:
o: Defending against any threat whatsoever
Inflicting MORE HARM than necessary for the purpose of defence
Defending one's own body
Defending against theft
questions.src: Section 37 explicitly caps the right — it never extends to more harm than necessary for the defensive purpose.

questions.q: Under Section 38 BNS, the right of private defence of the body extends to causing DEATH where the assault reasonably causes apprehension of:
o: Any minor inconvenience
Death, grievous hurt, rape, unnatural lust, kidnapping/abduction, or specified other serious threats
Only verbal insults
Only property damage
questions.src: Section 38 lists specific serious threat categories that justify lethal force in defence of the body.

questions.q: In Katta Surendra v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2008), the Supreme Court clarified that Exception 2 (exceeding private defence) to the murder provision applies only where:
o: The accused had absolutely no connection to any defensive situation
A GENUINE right of private defence existed, was exercised in good faith, and was exceeded without premeditation
The accused planned the act well in advance
The victim provoked the accused verbally only
questions.src: Katta Surendra confirmed Exception 2 requires an actual prior genuine right of defence, good faith, and absence of premeditation.

questions.q: Under Section 100 BNS (Culpable Homicide), death caused with the KNOWLEDGE that the act is likely to cause death is sufficient for the offence, requiring:
o: Proof of specific premeditated intention only, knowledge is irrelevant
EITHER intention to cause death/likely-fatal injury OR knowledge that the act is likely to cause death
Only accidental causation, with no fault element at all
Proof beyond all possible doubt of motive
questions.src: Section 100 recognises both intention-based and knowledge-based routes to culpable homicide liability.

questions.q: Under Section 101 BNS, culpable homicide amounts to MURDER when the act is done with the intention of causing bodily injury:
o: Of any kind whatsoever, however trivial
SUFFICIENT IN THE ORDINARY COURSE OF NATURE to cause death
Only to a child under 12 years
Only using a firearm
questions.src: This specific clause of Section 101 — injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death — is one of the four routes to murder.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five Exceptions to Section 101 (making culpable homicide NOT murder)?
o: Grave and sudden provocation
Sudden fight without premeditation
The offender being intoxicated voluntarily
Consent of the deceased (above 18 years) to the risk of death
questions.src: Voluntary intoxication is NOT one of the five recognised exceptions to murder; the actual five are provocation, exceeding private defence, public servant exceeding powers, sudden fight, and consent.

questions.q: Exception 5 to Section 101 BNS (consent) applies only where the deceased was:
o: Any age, with any form of consent
ABOVE 18 years of age, and voluntarily consented to the risk of death or to death itself
A close relative of the accused
Below 18 years of age
questions.src: Exception 5 specifically requires the deceased to be above 18 and to have genuinely, voluntarily consented.

questions.q: Section 103(2) BNS, a genuinely NEW provision not found in the original IPC, addresses:
o: Ordinary single-perpetrator murder
Murder committed by FIVE OR MORE persons on grounds like caste, race, community, or personal belief (mob lynching)
Only murders committed by police officers
Only murders occurring during a national emergency
questions.src: Section 103(2) is a new BNS provision specifically targeting group/mob-based murders motivated by identity-based grounds.

questions.q: Under the BNS, "Grievous Hurt" (as distinguished from ordinary "Hurt") includes specified categories such as:
o: Any momentary discomfort
Permanent privation of sight/hearing, fracture/dislocation of a bone, or hurt causing severe pain/inability to pursue ordinary activities for a specified period (20 days)
Only hurt caused by a specific named weapon
Only hurt causing immediate death
questions.src: Grievous Hurt is a specifically enumerated, more serious category than ordinary Hurt, covering these listed severe categories.

questions.q: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt specifically to DETER A PUBLIC SERVANT from discharge of duty is treated as:
o: Identical to ordinary hurt, with no distinction
A genuinely AGGRAVATED, separately punishable form of the offence
Not an offence at all
Only a civil wrong, never criminal
questions.src: This specific aggravated form recognises the additional harm to public order/justice administration when a public servant is targeted.

questions.q: Causing grievous hurt by throwing or administering ACID is treated under the BNS as:
o: Identical to ordinary grievous hurt with no separate provision
A separately, specifically defined and heavily punished offence, reflecting the severity of acid-attack crimes
A minor offence with lenient punishment
Not covered under the BNS at all
questions.src: Acid-attack provisions receive dedicated, heavily punitive treatment separate from ordinary grievous hurt provisions.

questions.q: "Wrongful Restraint," as distinguished from "Wrongful Confinement," involves:
o: Restricting a person within specific bounded limits
Obstructing a person so as to prevent them proceeding in a direction they have a right to proceed in — a comparatively less serious offence
Only applies to vehicles, never pedestrians
The same exact legal consequences as confinement
questions.src: Wrongful restraint is about blocking a direction of movement, less serious than wrongful confinement's bounded-limits restriction.

questions.q: "Assault," as distinguished from actual "Criminal Force," is essentially defined by:
o: Only actual physical contact occurring
A gesture or preparation intending/knowing it is likely to cause apprehension that criminal force is about to be used
Only verbal statements, never physical gestures
Requiring the victim to actually be touched
questions.src: Assault is about creating apprehension of imminent force, distinct from criminal force (actual force applied) or hurt (actual injury caused).

questions.q: "Kidnapping from Lawful Guardianship" applies to:
o: Any adult, taken with their full consent
A MINOR (under a specified age) or person of unsound mind, taken/enticed out of the keeping of their lawful guardian without the guardian's consent
Only kidnapping occurring outside India
Only kidnapping by strangers, never family members
questions.src: This specific form of kidnapping protects minors/persons of unsound mind by requiring the lawful guardian's consent for their removal.

questions.q: Under the Kidnapping vs Abduction distinction, "Abduction" alone (without any further accompanying intent) is:
o: Always a complete, independently punishable offence
NOT by itself a substantive offence — it requires an accompanying specific intent (e.g., intent to murder, to compel marriage) to become punishable
Identical to kidnapping in every legal respect
Only applicable to minors
questions.src: Unlike kidnapping (a substantive offence by itself), abduction requires proof of an accompanying specific criminal intent to attract punishment.

questions.q: For consent to be a valid general exception under the BNS, the person consenting must generally be capable of consenting AND the harm must:
o: Always automatically excuse any resulting death, without limitation
Not be intended or known to be likely to cause death (subject to the narrow Exception 5 to Section 101 for specific circumstances)
Never require any capacity to consent at all
Only apply to property offences, never bodily harm
questions.src: General consent as a defence has real limits — it does not ordinarily excuse causing death, except very narrowly under the specific murder-exception framework.

questions.q: "Necessity" as a general exception under the BNS excuses an act done:
o: For any personal convenience whatsoever
In GOOD FAITH, without criminal intention, to prevent or avoid OTHER harm to person or property
Only by government officials
Only in cases involving property, never personal harm
questions.src: The necessity exception requires genuine good faith and a real purpose of avoiding greater harm, not a pretext for otherwise-unlawful conduct.
